title: Day 2 Check: Creational Patterns & Strategy
summary: When to reach for Factory, Builder, Singleton and Strategy, and when not to.

questions.q: Why is double-checked locking in Java broken without `volatile` on the instance field?
options: `synchronized` doesn't work on static methods
Without a happens-before edge, another thread can see a non-null reference to a partially constructed object
The JVM forbids lazy initialisation
Two locks get created
questions.explain: The write of the reference can be reordered before the constructor's writes. `volatile` (or the holder idiom) gives safe publication.

questions.q: The interviewer asks: "There's only one ParkingLot, so should it be a Singleton?" Best answer?
options: Yes, always. That's what Singleton is for
No. I'd create one instance in `main` and inject it. A Singleton is hidden global state that makes testing and multi-lot support harder. I can show the thread-safe version if you want the pattern
No. Use a static class with static methods instead
Yes, but with `enum`
questions.explain: "Only one" is a wiring decision. Show you know the pattern and its costs.

questions.q: You need to support card, UPI and wallet now, with more methods added by other teams later. Which design scores best?
options: A `switch` on the method string inside `CheckoutService`
An abstract factory for payment families
A registry factory: `Map<method, constructor>` filled at startup, returning a `PaymentProcessor` interface
One class per method, each a Singleton
questions.explain: A registry lets new methods plug in without editing existing code (Open/Closed), and callers depend only on the interface.

questions.q: An object has 2 required and 7 optional fields and must be immutable. The idiomatic choice in Go is…
options: A constructor with 9 parameters
Exported fields that callers set after construction
Functional options: `New(required..., opts ...Option)`
A Builder struct with setter methods that return errors
questions.explain: Functional options are the Go equivalent of Builder (`grpc.Dial`, many std/x libraries). They keep defaults in one place and are easy to extend.

questions.q: Which signal in a problem statement most strongly suggests **Strategy**?
options: "There must be exactly one instance"
"Users can undo the last action"
"Pricing may be hourly, flat or surge-based, and we'll add more models"
"Notify all subscribers when the price changes"
questions.explain: Interchangeable algorithms behind one interface is Strategy. Undo is Command, notify-all is Observer, exactly-one is Singleton.

questions.q: What's the key difference between Strategy and State?
options: There's none. They're the same pattern
With Strategy the client picks the algorithm. With State the object swaps its own behaviour object as its internal state changes
State uses inheritance, Strategy uses static methods
Strategy is only for sorting
questions.explain: Their structure is similar. The intent and who triggers the change differ.

questions.q: In the discounts exercise, `Checkout` received a `List<DiscountStrategy>`. Adding a new 'first-order 15% off' promotion requires…
options: Editing `Checkout.total`
Adding a new strategy class and passing it in. `Checkout` doesn't change
Adding a new enum value and a switch case
Subclassing `Checkout`
questions.explain: That's the whole point. The extension is a new class, and the context stays closed for modification.

questions.q: Why should a Builder copy collections in the built object's constructor (e.g. `Map.copyOf`)?
options: For performance
So that later changes to the builder, or to the caller's map, can't change an object that's supposed to be immutable
Because Java requires it
To sort the keys
questions.explain: Immutability needs defensive copies on the way in and unmodifiable views (or copies) on the way out.
